disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through certain forms of indirect exposure. It is characterized by a pattern of intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative changes in cognition and mood, and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity, persisting for more than one month and causing significant distress or functional impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with onset sometimes delayed, and symptoms often fluctuating in intensity in response to triggers or life stress. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of trauma-linked re-experiencing and avoidance.

narrative.stressor: Four and a half months ago, on his way back from an early-morning run along the Salish Sea, Sigfredo was riding in a friend's car when they were struck at high speed by a drunk driver who ran a red light on the outskirts of Blaine. His friend in the driver’s seat was critically injured and trapped in the vehicle, and Sigfredo was stuck next to him for several minutes until first responders arrived, witnessing frantic efforts to stabilize his friend and the chaotic scene around them. Initially, Sigfredo focused on being "practical"—helping his parents with insurance calls, keeping his job at the telecom company, and visiting his friend in rehab—while downplaying how shaken he felt, especially in front of his close-knit family and church community. Over the next four months, however, the impact crept into his work, as he started avoiding driving, turning down weekend hikes that required highway travel, and struggling to stay present on customer calls, until his supervisor gently suggested employee counseling after noticing his frequent schedule changes and he agreed to see a mental health provider at the community clinic.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the car crash, it’s like the accident keeps replaying in my head when I’m awake and when I’m trying to relax, and I can’t shut it off.”

narrative.stressor: About five months ago, while performing a routine inspection at an aging warehouse renovation, Sherry was inside when a partially demolished mezzanine suddenly failed, sending a section of flooring and shelving crashing down just a few feet from where she had been standing moments earlier. She was pinned briefly by debris, heard a coworker screaming, and watched as emergency crews extracted an injured laborer with serious crush injuries; subsequent investigations and legal reviews heavily scrutinized her reports and decisions, leaving her feeling simultaneously blamed and terrified by how close she had come to being killed. In the months following the incident, her previously confident, meticulous approach to inspections deteriorated—she began avoiding certain types of sites, taking excessive time to complete reports, and turning down travel assignments, while at home her husband noticed she was increasingly tense, withdrawn, and preoccupied with worst-case scenarios. When she finally froze during a follow-up inspection at a similar warehouse and had to leave the site, her supervisor, concerned about both her safety and performance, recommended she speak with Occupational Health, which led to a referral for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since that collapse on the job, I can’t bring myself to go into certain buildings or walk under unfinished structures without feeling like I have to get out immediately.”

narrative.stressor: Six months ago, Henry collapsed at a small commercial job site after receiving a severe electrical shock when a supposedly de-energized panel turned out to be live, leaving him on the floor unable to move his right arm while coworkers shouted and waited for paramedics. He spent several days in the hospital for cardiac monitoring and treatment of burns, during which he was repeatedly told how close he had come to a fatal arrhythmia; afterward, he was cleared physically but given strict warnings about rest and follow-up. Initially, he joked about the incident with his crew and at trivia night, insisting he was fine, but over the following four months he began dodging higher-voltage work, snapping at apprentices over minor safety lapses, and taking on more paperwork and planning to avoid being the one directly on the panel. When his foreman noticed that Henry, usually the first to volunteer for complex installs, was now stalling on key tasks and coming up with excuses to stay off certain jobs, and Henry himself realized his work pride and social life were slipping, he accepted a suggestion from his primary care doctor to see a mental health specialist during a routine follow-up visit.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since I got shocked on that job, I feel this constant sense of dread and uneasiness that just won’t go away, even when I’m not at work.”
